draft.title: Voice as a literary device
card: Voice is the personality that comes through in the way a speaker or narrator tells something. A writer builds it through choices, so two speakers can describe the same event and sound very different.
the words chosen. "Grabbed" and "selected" can describe the same act, but they sound like different people.
the pattern of sentence length and pace. Short, broken sentences can sound nervous or angry. Long, flowing ones can sound calm or dreamy.

attitude is the speaker's feeling about the subject, such as scorn or affection. Point of view is who tells the story, such as "I" or an outside narrator. Together, these choices can make readers trust a speaker, pity them or doubt them.
draft.remember: A voice is built from word choice, rhythm, attitude and point of view, and it can guide how far readers trust the speaker.

a.q: Which choice by a writer is a choice of diction, one of the ways of building a voice?
opts: Calling a house a "shack" instead of a "home"
Using mostly short sentences in a tense scene
Telling the story as "I" instead of as an outside narrator
Having the speaker show scorn for the subject
a.why: Diction means the words chosen, and "shack" instead of "home" is a word choice. Short sentences are rhythm, "I" is point of view, and scorn is attitude, so the other options are other tools of voice.
a.clue: Diction is about the individual words picked.

b.q: A narrator says: "I wasn't late. Everyone else was early. Ask anyone." Then the narrator adds, "Actually, don't." What is the likely effect of this voice on a reader?
opts: Readers may doubt the narrator's honesty
Readers may pity a narrator who is very calm
Readers may trust the narrator's balanced view
Readers may see an outside narrator describing events
b.why: The defensive tone and the quick change of mind make the narrator sound as if they are hiding something, so readers may doubt them. The narrator says "I", so the outside-narrator option is wrong, and the voice is not calm or balanced.
b.clue: Notice the narrator's attitude and how the short sentences sound.

a.best: Calling a house a "shack" instead of a "home"

b.best: Readers may doubt the narrator's honesty
